title: Produce, don't possess
hook: the Tao gives birth and nourishes, but doesn't possess (Tao Te Ching 51)

segments.voice: Yesterday, no place for the tiger: claws need a handhold. Your line was no place for claws. What sharp thing found less to grab yesterday? Day one thousand one hundred thirteen.

A week of chapters ends today. Great skill that looks clumsy. Knowing what is enough. Knowing the world without going out the door. Subtracting a little each day. A mind with no fixed position. A traveler with no handhold for the tiger. Under all of them runs one quiet thread: less grabbing. Chapter fifty-one takes that thread to the very source of things. It asks what the Tao itself does with everything it brings to life. And the answer sounds like a parent at the curb on the first day of school, waving, and then driving away.
screen: `A WEEK OF LESS GRABBING.` → `WHAT DOES THE SOURCE DO?` → `A WAVE AT THE CURB.`

segments.voice: First, the making. The chapter says all things come from the Tao and are nourished by its virtue, its power, the Te in Tao Te Ching. Then they take shape and are brought to completion. Things grow, in this picture, because something gives and keeps on giving. Second, the honor. Everything honors the Tao, the chapter says, but not because anyone ordered it to. Nobody issues a decree. The respect simply arises, the way people come to trust a well that has never run dry. Third, the line that gives today its title. In James Legge's translation: "It produces them and makes no claim to the possession of them." And it keeps going in the same rhythm. It carries things along and doesn't boast about it. It brings them to maturity and doesn't control them. The chapter calls this the mysterious virtue. The source gives life, and then lets go of the thing it gave life to. Fourth, closer to home. Making something and wanting to own it can arrive as a single motion. The project with our name on it. The kid who should turn out the way we planned. The friend we helped, who ought to remember. The chapter doesn't say stop making, stop raising, stop helping. It says do all of it, fully, and then don't hold the deed. A garden grows better when the gardener stops pulling up the seedlings to check the roots.
screen: `ALL THINGS COME FROM THE TAO.` · `HONORED WITHOUT ANY DECREE.` · `IT PRODUCES, AND DOESN'T POSSESS.` · `MAKE IT FULLY, THEN DON'T HOLD THE DEED.` · then, large: `THE MYSTERIOUS VIRTUE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: help something grow, and let it go. Sit comfortably and let your breath slow. Bring to mind one thing you've helped along lately. A plant, a project, a person, a younger colleague, a child. See it as it is now, a little further on than before. Notice any wish to steer it, to be thanked, to have it turn out your way. You don't have to push that wish away. Just set it down beside you for these two minutes, and let the thing you helped be its own. The bell holds the time.
Produce. In chapter fifty-one, the Tao produces all things and makes no claim to own them. It gives life, and doesn't grab what it gave. Today's word.
Your line: don't possess. Help one thing along today, then step back without asking for credit or control. Day one thousand one hundred thirteen.

howItsDone: Readers of the Tao Te Ching often take chapter fifty-one as a model for parents, teachers and leaders: give fully, nourish, and then let what you helped become its own.

myth: chapter fifty-one says the Tao controls what it brings to maturity
it says the opposite: it brings things to maturity and doesn't control them.
the chapter says all things honor the Tao without being ordered to
nobody issues a decree; the honor simply arises.
the chapter tells people to stop making things
it pictures a source that produces fully and then lets go of what it made.

fork.setup: you're the source in chapter fifty-one. you've given life to something and seen it grow. what now?
options: let it go and don't boast.
fork.reveal: the Tao produces things and makes no claim to own them, carries them along without boasting, and brings them to maturity without control.

original.note: Chinese: it gives life and does not possess, from chapter fifty-one.

trapdoor: what you thought: produce, don't possess sounds like advice for a factory.
what it means: the source of things gives life fully, then lets what it made be its own.
what a scholar hears: the chapter names this the mysterious virtue, and the same refrain of giving without owning also closes chapter ten.

notes: Editor pass: removed 'you trust' (telling the listener what they feel) and replaced the recurring 'an ordinary Tuesday' turn.

Day 1113 is a week end (days 1107-1113); the hook names the week's chapters from the index titles (seems clumsy, content with enough, without going out the door, daily decrease, no fixed mind, no place for the tiger), since the scripts for days 1107-1111 were not on disk when this was written. Check the look-back matches those days.
Trapdoor claims the giving-without-owning refrain (生而不有，為而不恃，長而不宰，是謂玄德) also closes chapter 10. Confirm against the received text.
Original 生而不有 (shēng ér bù yǒu) rendered 'SHUNG er boo YO'; confirm.
The well, parent at the curb and gardener images are the writer's illustrations, not the text's.
